item.content:encoded:
The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 is a fully funded, 10-week research fellowship in Cambridge, United Kingdom, designed for talented researchers, professionals, policymakers, and individuals from diverse academic and professional backgrounds who want to work on some of the most important challenges surrounding advanced artificial intelligence.

The Winter 2027 cohort will begin on 18 January 2027 and will provide selected fellows with financial support, expert mentorship, research assistance, networking opportunities, and access to a community working at the intersection of AI safety, AI governance, technical research, and public policy.

With a £10,000 stipend, visa support, meals during working hours, and travel expense coverage, the fellowship offers participants an opportunity to spend 10 weeks developing a substantial research project while working alongside experienced researchers and mentors in Cambridge.

Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 at a Glance

  • Opportunity: Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship
  • Cohort: Winter 2027
  • Location: Cambridge, United Kingdom
  • Duration: 10 weeks
  • Start date: 18 January 2027
  • Stipend: £10,000
  • Funding: Fully funded
  • Application deadline: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Anywhere on Earth
  • Minimum age: 18 years
  • Application: Online
  • Research areas: Technical AI Safety, AI Governance, and Technical AI Governance
  • Mentorship: Yes
  • Visa support: Yes
  • Travel support: Yes
  • Meals: Provided during working hours
  • Potential continuation: 6+ month fully funded Research Scholars positions may be available to top fellows

What Is the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship?

The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship is a 10-week research programme hosted in Cambridge, UK. It is focused on helping talented individuals investigate ways of reducing risks associated with increasingly capable and autonomous AI systems.

The programme brings together people from different disciplines and professional backgrounds. Rather than limiting applications to individuals with a particular degree, nationality, profession, or academic credential, ERA takes a talent-first approach.

Participants are expected to develop a research project addressing important questions in frontier AI safety, AI governance, or technical mechanisms that can make AI governance more effective.

The fellowship is particularly relevant as artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable and are being integrated into areas ranging from scientific research and cybersecurity to public administration, business, education, and national security.

What Does the Fellowship Provide?

One of the major attractions of the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship is that fellows are provided with extensive financial and professional support throughout the programme.

1. £10,000 Fellowship Stipend

Selected fellows receive a £10,000 stipend for the 10-week fellowship.

This financial support allows participants to dedicate substantial time to their research without having to treat the fellowship as an unpaid professional commitment.

2. Visa Support

For international fellows who require permission to participate in the programme in the United Kingdom, ERA provides visa support.

This is particularly important for applicants based outside the UK who want to participate in the in-person fellowship in Cambridge.

3. Travel Expense Coverage

The fellowship also provides support for travel expenses, helping reduce the financial barriers associated with travelling to Cambridge for the programme.

4. Meal Provisions

Fellows receive meal provisions during working hours, providing additional practical support during the 10-week programme.

5. Expert Mentorship

Each fellow works closely with a mentor during the fellowship.

Mentorship is an important component of the programme because participants are expected to develop and complete a meaningful research project. Mentors can provide guidance on research questions, methodology, project development, academic direction, and the broader implications of the fellow’s work.

ERA notes that mentors differ between cohorts. Fellows are matched with mentors after acceptance according to their research interests and needs.

Previous ERA mentors have included researchers and experts associated with organisations across academia, government, industry, and AI safety.

6. Research Management Support

Fellows receive dedicated research management support throughout their projects.

This support is intended to help participants become stronger researchers and policymakers in the AI safety and governance space.

The fellowship’s alumni have gone on to publish research in prominent academic venues, including conferences such as NeurIPS.

7. Cambridge Research Community

Participants become part of a community of people working on difficult questions related to advanced AI.

During the fellowship, fellows have access to a dedicated desk space at ERA’s Cambridge office and participate in regular social events and community activities.

This creates opportunities to exchange ideas, receive feedback, collaborate, and build professional relationships.

8. Networking and Career Development

ERA also helps fellows develop the skills, expertise, and networks necessary for careers in AI safety and AI policy.

The organisation can facilitate introductions to relevant organisations and professionals working in the field.

In exceptional cases, ERA may also provide additional financial assistance to support particularly impactful career transitions.

9. Potential Long-Term Research Opportunities

The fellowship can also serve as a pathway to longer-term research.

Top-performing fellows may have the opportunity to continue their work through ERA’s Research Scholars programme, which offers six months or longer of full-time funded positions.

This means that the 10-week fellowship can potentially become the beginning of a much longer research career in AI safety or governance.

Who Can Apply for the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship?

One of the most distinctive aspects of this fellowship is its broad eligibility policy.

Anyone aged 18 or older can apply.

ERA describes the programme as talent-first and states that it cares about much more than conventional credentials. There are no formal eligibility restrictions beyond being at least 18 years old.

Applicants therefore do not necessarily need to come from a traditional computer science or artificial intelligence background.

The programme welcomes people with different forms of expertise, provided they have the ability, motivation, and potential to contribute meaningfully to the mission of reducing risks associated with advanced AI.

Who Is Particularly Encouraged to Apply?

Although the fellowship is open broadly, it may be especially valuable for the following groups.

Researchers at Any Career Stage

Researchers can apply if they want to:

  • Apply their existing expertise to high-priority AI safety or governance questions.
  • Explore a new research direction.
  • Work across disciplinary boundaries.
  • Develop research relevant to advanced AI systems.
  • Redirect an existing research programme toward frontier AI challenges.

The programme is not restricted to senior academics. Researchers at different stages of their careers may be considered.

Professionals from Technical and Policy Fields

Professionals working in areas such as:

  • Technology
  • Computer science
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Public policy
  • Government
  • National security
  • Security studies
  • Law
  • Economics
  • Research
  • Governance
  • Regulation
  • Other relevant disciplines

may find the fellowship particularly valuable.

The programme provides an opportunity to apply existing professional expertise to emerging problems associated with increasingly capable AI systems.

People Redirecting Their Research Careers

The fellowship can also suit individuals who already have a research agenda but want to shift their work toward advanced AI safety and governance.

For example, someone with expertise in economics, cybersecurity, law, international relations, public administration, or computer science could use the fellowship to investigate how that discipline can contribute to managing risks from frontier AI.

Individuals with Distinctive Domain Expertise

ERA is also interested in applicants who bring unusual or underrepresented perspectives.

An applicant does not necessarily need to be an AI specialist if they possess expertise that could improve society’s understanding of advanced AI risks or contribute to developing effective solutions.

What Will Fellows Research?

During the fellowship, participants develop and complete a research project focused on technical and/or governance measures for mitigating risks posed by frontier AI systems.

Fellows receive support from:

  • ERA research managers
  • Individual mentors
  • ERA’s wider institutional network
  • Researchers and experts from relevant organisations

ERA supports research across the full range of frontier AI governance and technical AI safety.

Its wider research network includes experts associated with organisations such as the University of Cambridge, UK AI Security Institute, Centre for the Governance of AI, RAND Corporation, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic, among others.

The research programme is divided broadly into three streams.

1. Technical AI Safety

The technical stream focuses on understanding increasingly capable AI systems and developing methods to ensure that humans can maintain meaningful control and oversight.

As AI systems become more autonomous, researchers need to understand what these systems can do, how they behave, what capabilities they may develop, and how to prevent harmful or unpredictable outcomes.

ERA supports technical research in areas including:

  • AI evaluations
  • Interpretability
  • Robustness
  • Alignment
  • AI control
  • Dangerous capability detection
  • Model behaviour monitoring
  • Safeguards
  • Human oversight
  • AI system reliability

Research may involve investigating how to measure or elicit potentially dangerous capabilities, understanding the internal workings of AI models, designing stronger safeguards, monitoring model behaviour, and developing techniques for controlling systems whose objectives may not fully align with those of their operators.

The programme is also interested in emerging challenges such as:

  • Detecting deceptive or strategically evasive AI behaviour.
  • Controlling AI systems capable of automating parts of AI research and development.
  • Accelerating alignment research across the LLM training stack.
  • Developing safeguards that remain effective as AI models become increasingly capable.

The overall objective is to contribute to the development of AI systems that can remain subject to effective human oversight while incorporating appropriate safeguards against harmful or unpredictable behaviour.

2. AI Governance

The governance stream focuses on how governments, companies, international institutions, and other organisations should manage increasingly capable AI systems.

As frontier AI becomes more powerful, decisions regarding its development and deployment become increasingly consequential.

Effective governance requires institutions that can:

  • Understand rapidly changing AI risks.
  • Develop credible rules and safeguards.
  • Hold powerful AI developers accountable.
  • Coordinate across national borders.
  • Respond to emerging technological developments.
  • Build effective regulatory systems.

ERA supports research in areas such as:

  • Regulatory design
  • Regulatory implementation
  • Frontier AI safety frameworks
  • Corporate governance
  • Accountability
  • International coordination
  • AI policy
  • Institutional capacity

Researchers in this stream may investigate how governments and other institutions can develop governance systems that keep pace with technological progress.

Potential research questions may involve increasingly autonomous AI agents, international coordination, frontier AI regulation, and the development of security and verification systems for advanced AI.

The broader goal is to help institutions adapt as AI capabilities and associated risks change.

3. Technical AI Governance

Technical AI governance sits at the intersection of AI technology, governance, regulation, measurement, and verification.

The central idea is that effective AI governance cannot depend entirely on companies voluntarily reporting what their systems can do or how they were developed.

Governments and other stakeholders need reliable technical mechanisms for determining:

  • What AI systems are capable of.
  • How much computing power they use.
  • Where systems are deployed.
  • How systems are developed.
  • Whether regulatory requirements are being followed.
  • Whether claims made by AI developers can be independently verified.

ERA therefore supports research involving:

  • Compute governance
  • AI auditing
  • AI monitoring
  • Hardware-enabled verification
  • Technical standards
  • Measurement
  • Privacy-preserving verification
  • AI system auditing

Potential research could explore how regulators can identify AI systems that cross important risk thresholds, how hardware and computing infrastructure can enable verification while protecting privacy, and how increasingly autonomous systems can be monitored.

This field is particularly important because policymakers may create effective regulations but struggle to implement them if they lack the technical infrastructure needed to measure compliance.

ERA’s objective is to help develop governance systems based on credible measurement, verification, and enforcement rather than relying solely on trust or self-reporting.

Why Is the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Important?

The rapid development of frontier AI has created a growing need for people who can understand both the opportunities and risks associated with increasingly capable systems.

AI safety is not solely a computer science problem. It involves questions concerning:

  • Public policy
  • Economics
  • International relations
  • Law
  • Security
  • Ethics
  • Governance
  • Computer science
  • Engineering
  • Institutional design
  • Regulation

This makes interdisciplinary expertise increasingly valuable.

The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship provides an environment in which individuals from different backgrounds can bring their knowledge to emerging questions surrounding advanced AI.

For someone considering a career in AI safety, AI governance, technology policy, or related research, the fellowship can provide an opportunity to gain specialised experience while building connections with researchers and institutions working in the field.

Application Process for the Winter 2027 Fellowship

Applications for the Winter 2027 Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship are currently open.

The selection process consists of several stages.

Stage 1: Written Application

The first stage primarily consists of short essay questions.

ERA estimates that applicants should spend approximately two hours completing this stage.

The written application is an important opportunity for candidates to demonstrate their thinking, motivation, research ability, and potential contribution to AI safety or governance.

Applicants should therefore approach the essays carefully rather than treating them as a simple administrative form.

Stage 2: First Interview

Following the written application stage, approximately the top 20% of candidates will be invited to first-round interviews.

These interviews are scheduled to take place in late September 2026.

Candidates should be prepared to discuss their interests, experience, reasoning, and potential research directions.

Stage 3: Second Interview

Applicants who are particularly promising after the first interview may be invited to a shorter second-round interview.

When candidates are invited to this stage, ERA will also contact their references.

Second-round interviews are expected to take place in early October 2026.

Stage 4: Offers and Research Development

Following the selection process, successful applicants will receive acceptance offers.

After offers are made, ERA will work with the selected fellows to develop their project ideas and match them with appropriate mentors.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to arrive with a completely finalised research proposal. The fellowship provides an environment in which project ideas can be refined with support from research managers and mentors.

Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Deadline

The application deadline for the Winter 2027 Fellowship is:

13 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Anywhere on Earth (AoE).

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their applications.

Because the deadline is expressed in Anywhere on Earth time, applicants should verify the corresponding deadline in their local time zone and submit well in advance.

How to Apply for the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship

Interested applicants can submit their application through the official application form.

Applicants should carefully review the application questions and provide clear, thoughtful responses demonstrating their suitability for the fellowship.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although the fellowship is talent-first and does not impose traditional academic eligibility requirements, applicants should still demonstrate why they are capable of making a meaningful contribution.

1. Clearly Explain Your Interest in Advanced AI

Show that you understand why AI safety and governance matter and explain what motivates you to work on these issues.

2. Connect Your Existing Expertise to AI

You do not necessarily need an AI degree.

Instead, explain how your current knowledge could contribute to AI safety, governance, or technical AI governance.

For example, a lawyer could explore AI regulation, an economist could investigate AI incentives and governance, a cybersecurity professional could examine AI security, while a political scientist could investigate international coordination.

3. Demonstrate Strong Research Thinking

The fellowship is fundamentally research-oriented.

Applicants should demonstrate an ability to identify important questions, think critically, analyse evidence, and develop useful approaches to complex problems.

4. Identify Potential Research Directions

While a fully developed proposal may not be required, having some ideas about the problems you would like to investigate can strengthen your application.

Think about questions that are:

  • Important
  • Relevant to frontier AI
  • Researchable
  • Potentially impactful
  • Connected to your existing expertise

5. Highlight Your Distinctive Perspective

ERA specifically welcomes people with distinctive domain expertise and perspectives.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that they must compete by presenting themselves as conventional AI researchers.

Your unique professional or academic background may be one of your greatest strengths.

6. Take the Essay Questions Seriously

The written application is the first major stage of selection.

Because the programme expects applicants to spend around two hours on the essays, candidates should dedicate sufficient time to developing thoughtful and well-structured responses.

7. Prepare for Interviews

Candidates selected for interviews should be ready to explain:

  • Why they are interested in AI safety or governance.
  • What research questions interest them.
  • How their existing expertise could contribute.
  • How they approach difficult and uncertain problems.
  • What they hope to accomplish during the fellowship.

Location and Fellowship Experience

The fellowship is hosted in Cambridge, United Kingdom.

Fellows will have dedicated desk space at the ERA office and will participate in community activities and social events.

The in-person environment provides opportunities to interact with other researchers and professionals while working on individual projects.

Cambridge also provides a strong academic and research environment, making it a particularly relevant location for individuals interested in advanced technology, public policy, and interdisciplinary research.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship may be particularly suitable for someone who:

  • Wants to transition into AI safety research.
  • Is already conducting research and wants to explore advanced AI questions.
  • Works in technology or engineering.
  • Has expertise in public policy or government.
  • Works in law or regulation.
  • Has a background in economics.
  • Works in national security or cybersecurity.
  • Wants to develop expertise in AI governance.
  • Has interdisciplinary research interests.
  • Possesses distinctive expertise that could contribute to understanding AI risks.
  • Wants to build a professional network in AI safety and governance.
  • Is interested in pursuing a longer-term research career.

Because the fellowship has no formal eligibility restrictions beyond the minimum age requirement, applicants should not automatically exclude themselves because they do not have a traditional AI background.

APPLY HERE

International Eligibility and Nationality

The fellowship states that anyone can apply, provided they are 18 years or older.

There is no stated restriction limiting applications to a particular race, nationality, country, or continent.

Therefore, applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, and other parts of the world may apply, subject to meeting the programme’s general requirements and being able to participate in the fellowship in Cambridge.

The fellowship’s broad approach means that applicants from countries across the Global South and Global North can potentially be considered.

International applicants should also take into account the practical requirements associated with travelling to and participating in a 10-week programme in the United Kingdom. ERA states that it provides visa support and travel expense coverage for fellows.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 in the UK.

Key Reasons to Consider the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship

The fellowship combines several elements that can be difficult to access through conventional research opportunities:

  1. A £10,000 stipend for the 10-week programme.
  2. Visa support for eligible international participants.
  3. Travel expense coverage.
  4. Meals during working hours.
  5. One-to-one mentorship.
  6. Dedicated research management support.
  7. Access to a Cambridge-based research community.
  8. Networking opportunities across AI safety and governance.
  9. Opportunities to develop research that can potentially lead to academic publication.
  10. Potential access to 6+ month funded Research Scholars positions for top fellows.

The combination of financial support, mentorship, research experience, and professional networking makes the programme particularly relevant for individuals seeking to build a long-term career in AI safety or governance.

Conclusion

The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 offers an intensive 10-week opportunity for talented individuals to work on some of the world’s most important emerging questions surrounding advanced artificial intelligence.

The programme is particularly notable for its talent-first approach. Rather than restricting applications to a narrow academic discipline or professional background, ERA welcomes people with diverse expertise who can contribute to understanding and addressing frontier AI risks.

Successful fellows will receive a £10,000 stipend, visa support, travel expense coverage, meals during working hours, expert mentorship, research management assistance, workspace in Cambridge, networking opportunities, and access to a wider community working on AI safety and governance.

Research opportunities cover three major areas: Technical AI Safety, AI Governance, and Technical AI Governance. These streams address challenges ranging from AI alignment and interpretability to regulation, international coordination, auditing, monitoring, compute governance, and technical verification.

The programme is open to applicants aged 18 and above from any country or region, with no stated nationality, race, or continental restrictions. Applicants from technical, policy, legal, economic, security, research, and other relevant backgrounds are encouraged to consider applying.

For the Winter 2027 cohort, the fellowship begins on 18 January 2027, while applications close on 13 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Anywhere on Earth.

For candidates interested in building a research career focused on the safe development, governance, and responsible management of increasingly capable AI systems, the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship could provide a valuable platform to develop expertise, conduct meaningful research, establish professional connections, and potentially continue into longer-term funded research.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are open for the Fall 2026 Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative Mentorship Program, an initiative designed to support prospective graduate students interested in pursuing PhD study in Political Science, Political Theory, and related areas of academic research.

The Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative (GSIDI) is a joint project led by Steve Teles of the Johns Hopkins University SNF Agora Institute and Jenna Storey of the American Enterprise Institute (AEI). The initiative seeks to broaden the range of intellectual perspectives represented within higher education by strengthening the pipeline of prospective scholars considering academic careers.

For its mentorship program, GSIDI is matching a select group of prospective graduate students with faculty members from leading PhD-granting institutions. Successful applicants will receive individualized guidance during the fall semester as they prepare applications for doctoral study.

The initiative is particularly interested in students whose research questions, hypotheses, theoretical perspectives, or approaches may be described as conservative, moderate, or heterodox liberal, as well as applicants interested more broadly in questions of intellectual diversity within academia.

Importantly, the initiative does not describe its faculty network as ideologically uniform. According to the program description, participating mentors include scholars from different political perspectives who share an interest in maintaining intellectual diversity within the academic research community.

The priority application deadline is September 15, 2026.

About the Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative

The Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative was created in response to concerns about the range of political and intellectual viewpoints represented within higher education.

The initiative argues that when certain perspectives are significantly underrepresented within academic disciplines, this can have consequences for the research process itself.

One concern highlighted by GSIDI is what it describes as “field compression.”

In this context, field compression refers to a situation where the range of:

  • Research questions being asked
  • Hypotheses being considered
  • Theoretical approaches being used
  • Interpretations being debated
  • Assumptions being questioned

may become narrower because certain intellectual or ideological perspectives are less frequently represented within a discipline.

GSIDI therefore focuses not only on existing university faculty but on the graduate-school pipeline that produces future academics.

The initiative aims to identify promising prospective scholars early in their academic journey and provide them with mentorship before and during the PhD application process.

Who Leads GSIDI?

The Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative is jointly led by:

Steve Teles

Steve Teles is affiliated with the SNF Agora Institute at Johns Hopkins University.

Jenna Storey

Jenna Storey is affiliated with the American Enterprise Institute.

Together, they have developed GSIDI as a program focused on strengthening intellectual diversity within higher education by supporting prospective graduate students.

The initiative has initially built a national network of scholars in:

  • Political Science
  • Political Theory

The organizers hope that the model may eventually inspire similar efforts in other academic fields, although the current program described in the supplied materials focuses specifically on these areas.

What Is the GSIDI Mentorship Program?

The GSIDI Mentorship Program matches selected prospective graduate students with established professors at highly ranked PhD-granting institutions.

These faculty members have agreed to serve as mentors because of their commitment to intellectual diversity within academic research and graduate education.

Successful applicants will receive advice over the course of the fall semester while preparing for graduate-school applications.

The program is therefore particularly relevant to students who are:

  • Planning to apply to PhD programs during Fall 2026
  • Interested in Political Science or Political Theory
  • Considering an academic career
  • Seeking guidance from experienced faculty members
  • Interested in research questions or approaches that may fall outside dominant intellectual perspectives within their field

What Mentors Will Help With

GSIDI mentors are expected to provide general guidance on several areas of academic development.

Graduate School Applications

One of the primary purposes of the mentorship is to help students navigate the PhD application process.

For prospective doctoral students, applying to graduate school can involve difficult decisions regarding:

  • Which programs to target
  • How to identify faculty fit
  • How to frame research interests
  • How to communicate academic potential
  • How to position an application strategically
  • How to understand differences among departments

A mentor who already understands graduate admissions and academic culture can provide valuable perspective during this process.

Academic Research Direction

Applicants will provide information about their research interests when applying.

This allows GSIDI to consider whether a prospective student can be matched with a faculty member whose expertise or academic experience is relevant to the applicant’s goals.

Mentorship may help candidates think more carefully about:

  • Research questions
  • Areas of specialization
  • Theoretical approaches
  • Intellectual positioning
  • Long-term academic interests

Peer-Reviewed Publications

The initiative states that mentors may also provide general advice concerning peer-reviewed publication.

For prospective academics, learning how scholarly publishing works can be important even before beginning a doctoral program.

Faculty mentors may help applicants better understand:

  • What academic journals are looking for
  • How research develops into publishable work
  • The role of peer review
  • How publication fits into an academic career
  • What kinds of research preparation are useful before beginning a PhD

The program description does not indicate that participants are guaranteed publication opportunities. Rather, mentors provide general advice about academic publishing.

Careers in Academia

GSIDI also provides guidance about the prospects of a career in higher education.

Applicants who are considering long-term careers as:

  • University professors
  • Academic researchers
  • Political scientists
  • Political theorists
  • Policy scholars

may benefit from realistic conversations with experienced faculty members about the structure of academic careers.

This could include discussions about graduate study, publishing, research agendas, academic hiring, and the long-term demands of university research.

Who Is the Program Designed For?

GSIDI is primarily designed for prospective graduate students who are actively applying to PhD programs.

The Fall 2026 application asks whether the applicant is currently applying for graduate school and is specifically aimed at students preparing applications during the fall admissions cycle.

The initiative is especially interested in candidates whose academic interests involve questions, hypotheses, or approaches that may be described as:

  • Conservative
  • Moderate
  • Heterodox liberal

However, this does not mean applicants must adopt a particular political identity.

The initiative’s language focuses primarily on intellectual approaches and research questions, rather than requiring applicants to identify personally with a specific political party or ideology.

Political Science and Political Theory Focus

The current GSIDI network has been launched primarily within:

Political Science

and:

Political Theory

The mentorship program connects prospective graduate students with professors at leading doctoral programs in these areas.

Applicants planning PhD research in adjacent fields should carefully consider whether their proposed doctoral work fits clearly within Political Science, Political Theory, or the participating scholars’ areas of expertise.

The supplied information does not state that the Fall 2026 mentorship program is currently open across all humanities and social-science disciplines.

Why GSIDI Focuses on Intellectual Diversity

The initiative is based on the view that academic research benefits when scholars approach questions from different intellectual traditions.

GSIDI argues that limited representation of center-right and other less common perspectives within some areas of higher education may narrow scholarly debate.

From the initiative’s perspective, improving intellectual diversity can increase the range of:

  • Questions researchers ask
  • Explanations scholars test
  • Competing hypotheses considered
  • Interpretive frameworks employed
  • Scholarly disagreements represented

The program therefore approaches intellectual diversity as an issue affecting both university culture and the research process.

Prospective applicants should understand this intellectual mission before applying and should be able to explain why the program is relevant to their own research interests.

Faculty Mentors

Successful applicants will be matched with faculty mentors from highly ranked PhD-granting institutions.

The initiative emphasizes that participating mentors are established scholars within Political Science and Political Theory.

Faculty participating in the network do not necessarily share the same political outlook.

Some may be conservative, while others may have liberal or other perspectives but support the principle that academic research should include a wider variety of intellectual viewpoints.

This is an important feature of the initiative: the mentorship is not described simply as ideological networking, but as an effort to connect prospective scholars with established academics committed to intellectual diversity.

How the Mentorship Works

The mentorship is intended to take place over the Fall 2026 semester.

The general process is:

  1. Prospective PhD applicants complete the GSIDI mentorship application.
  2. Applicants provide information about their academic background and research interests.
  3. Applicants upload their university transcript.
  4. GSIDI staff review the submitted materials.
  5. Selected applicants are matched with appropriate faculty mentors.
  6. Mentors provide advice as applicants prepare graduate-school applications during the fall.

The program description does not specify an exact number of mentorship meetings or a fixed number of hours participants will receive.

Applicants should therefore treat the mentorship as individualized academic guidance rather than a standardized course with a predetermined weekly schedule.

Application Requirements

The application appears intentionally straightforward compared with many fellowship or graduate-admissions applications.

Applicants are asked to provide information concerning their:

  • Academic background
  • Research interests
  • Graduate-school plans

They must also upload:

A copy of their university transcript

The program states that submitted materials will only be shared with:

  • GSIDI staff
  • Potential faculty mentors

Applicants should carefully complete the form so that organizers have sufficient information to identify an appropriate mentor.

University Transcript

Applicants must upload their university transcript as part of the application.

The information provided does not specify:

  • Whether an official transcript is required
  • Whether an unofficial transcript is acceptable
  • A minimum GPA
  • A particular degree classification

Applicants should therefore follow the instructions shown within the official application form.

Research Interests

Applicants will be asked to provide information about their research interests.

This is likely to be particularly important for mentor matching.

Candidates should be prepared to explain clearly:

  • What area of Political Science or Political Theory interests them
  • What research questions they may want to investigate
  • Why those questions matter
  • What intellectual or theoretical approaches interest them
  • What type of PhD program they hope to enter

A focused description can make it easier for GSIDI staff to understand where the applicant might benefit most from mentorship.

Applicants Should Be Preparing for PhD Applications

The program is not presented as a general undergraduate mentoring initiative.

The Fall 2026 call specifically asks for students who are currently applying to graduate school.

Applicants should therefore ideally be at the stage where they are preparing applications for PhD study during the upcoming admissions cycle.

This may involve activities such as:

  • Researching doctoral programs
  • Identifying potential supervisors
  • Preparing statements of purpose
  • Developing research interests
  • Requesting recommendation letters
  • Preparing academic writing samples
  • Reviewing transcripts
  • Considering future academic careers

Priority Application Deadline

The priority deadline is September 15, 2026.

Applicants should distinguish between a priority deadline and a final deadline.

The information provided specifies September 15 as the priority deadline but does not state a separate final closing date.

Candidates interested in the mentorship should therefore aim to submit their application by September 15, 2026 rather than assuming applications will remain open substantially later.

How to Apply

Prospective applicants should complete the official Fall 2026 GSIDI Mentorship Application.

The application asks candidates to provide details about their research background and academic interests and to upload a university transcript.

Information about the broader Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative is available through the Johns Hopkins University SNF Agora Institute website.

If you would like to receive updates about GSIDI news and events, please register HERE.

APPLY HERE

Questions About the Program

Applicants with questions can contact:

Jacob Bruggeman

Email:

Jbrugge2@jhu.edu

Prospective candidates may wish to contact the program if they are uncertain about whether their research area fits the current Political Science and Political Theory network.

GSIDI News and Events

Individuals who are interested in the initiative but are not yet applying to graduate school can also register to receive news and event updates.

This could be useful for:

  • Undergraduate students considering future graduate study
  • Master’s students planning to apply in a later cycle
  • Researchers interested in intellectual diversity
  • Students interested in academic careers

The updates form is separate from the formal mentorship application.

Tips for Preparing a Strong GSIDI Application

1. Explain Your Research Interests Clearly

Avoid describing your interests only in extremely broad terms such as “politics” or “democracy.”

Explain the questions you are actually curious about.

For example, identify:

  • A political institution
  • A theoretical problem
  • A policy question
  • A historical development
  • A research puzzle
  • A methodological challenge

that you may want to investigate.

2. Explain Why Intellectual Diversity Matters to Your Research

The initiative has a distinctive mission.

Applicants should therefore be able to explain why GSIDI’s emphasis on intellectual diversity is relevant to them.

The strongest explanation need not be ideological.

It could focus on:

  • Testing competing hypotheses
  • Challenging assumptions
  • Engaging opposing arguments
  • Expanding theoretical perspectives
  • Improving research design
  • Encouraging more rigorous debate

3. Avoid Treating Political Identity as the Entire Application

The initiative focuses on broadening intellectual perspectives, but applicants are still applying for academic mentorship.

A strong application should therefore demonstrate:

  • Serious research interests
  • Academic preparation
  • Intellectual curiosity
  • Interest in doctoral study
  • Potential for scholarly development

Political self-identification alone is unlikely to communicate sufficient academic potential.

4. Be Specific About Your PhD Plans

Explain where you are in the application process.

You may want to identify:

  • General subfield
  • Research topics
  • Types of programs
  • Career objectives

This can help GSIDI determine which faculty mentor may be most useful.

5. Prepare Your Transcript Early

Because the application requires a university transcript, obtain the appropriate document before beginning the final submission process.

6. Apply by the Priority Deadline

Aim for:

September 15, 2026

rather than waiting to see whether applications remain open afterward.

Why This Mentorship Can Be Valuable

PhD admissions differ considerably from undergraduate and many master’s admissions processes.

Applicants are often evaluated not only on grades but on:

  • Intellectual potential
  • Research fit
  • Academic writing
  • Research experience
  • Recommendation letters
  • Clarity of scholarly goals
  • Fit with faculty and departments

For students unfamiliar with academic institutions, understanding these expectations can be difficult.

A faculty mentor with experience in leading Political Science or Political Theory programs may help prospective applicants better understand how academic departments evaluate doctoral candidates.

The mentorship can also help students think beyond admission itself and consider whether a long-term career in academic research is genuinely appropriate for their goals.

What the Program Does Not Promise

Based on the information provided, GSIDI should not be described as guaranteeing:

  • Admission to a PhD program
  • Funding for doctoral study
  • A scholarship
  • A paid stipend
  • Employment
  • Publication
  • Placement at a specific university

Its central benefit is faculty mentorship and guidance.

Applicants should therefore understand it primarily as an academic-development and PhD-application mentorship opportunity.

Important Information at a Glance

Program: Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative Mentorship Program

Cycle: Fall 2026

Academic areas: Political Science and Political Theory

Organizers: Johns Hopkins University SNF Agora Institute and American Enterprise Institute-affiliated project leadership

Program leaders: Steve Teles and Jenna Storey

Target group: Prospective graduate students applying for PhD programs

Main activity: Faculty mentorship during the PhD application process

Mentor network: Professors at highly ranked PhD-granting institutions

Application materials: Background information, research interests, and university transcript

Priority deadline: September 15, 2026

Contact: Jbrugge2@jhu.edu

Conclusion

The Graduate Student Intellectual Diversity Initiative Mentorship Program Fall 2026 offers a distinctive opportunity for prospective Political Science and Political Theory PhD applicants seeking individualized guidance from established academics.

Led jointly by Steve Teles of the Johns Hopkins University SNF Agora Institute and Jenna Storey of the American Enterprise Institute, GSIDI seeks to strengthen intellectual diversity in higher education by focusing on the pipeline through which future university researchers and professors are trained.

Selected participants will be matched with faculty mentors from leading PhD-granting institutions and receive guidance during the fall graduate-school application cycle.

Mentors may advise participants on:

  • PhD applications
  • Academic research
  • Peer-reviewed publications
  • Graduate-school strategy
  • Careers in academia

The program is particularly intended for prospective scholars whose research questions, hypotheses, or approaches may be characterized as conservative, moderate, or heterodox liberal, although the faculty network itself includes scholars with different political viewpoints who share an interest in intellectual diversity.

Applicants should be preparing to apply to PhD programs during Fall 2026 and should be ready to provide information about their research interests, academic background, and university transcript.

The priority deadline is September 15, 2026.

For students considering a future in Political Science or Political Theory who want experienced academic guidance before submitting doctoral applications, GSIDI provides an opportunity to receive targeted mentorship during a particularly important stage of the academic career pipeline.

If you are currently applying for graduate school, and would like to be considered for this mentorship program, please fill out this FORM.

For more academic, fellowship, and graduate opportunities, VISIT HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The International Criminal Police Organization, better known as INTERPOL, has opened applications for its Enhanced Secondment Programme, a major international professional opportunity designed to strengthen global law enforcement cooperation by bringing qualified police officers, law enforcement specialists and government officials from INTERPOL Member Countries into its international operational environment.

The programme provides an opportunity for experienced law enforcement professionals to contribute their expertise to international efforts against transnational crime while gaining exposure to complex international policing operations, investigative techniques, advanced technologies and multinational cooperation.

The opportunity is based within INTERPOL’s operational structures, with the vacancy announcement indicating multiple duty stations and a secondment duration of 36 months. The programme is associated with Grade 5 positions and requires candidates to meet INTERPOL’s eligibility, professional experience, endorsement and security requirements.

According to the vacancy notice, the programme is intended to create a dynamic and secure pool of vetted law enforcement specialists who can be deployed or assigned according to operational needs, ensuring that the right expertise is available to address international crime challenges.

About the INTERPOL Enhanced Secondment Programme

INTERPOL is the world’s largest international police organization, with 196 member states. Established in 1923, the organization facilitates cross-border police cooperation and supports authorities and organizations whose missions involve preventing and combating international crime.

Through the Enhanced Secondment Programme, INTERPOL is seeking qualified law enforcement officers and experts who can strengthen its global operational capabilities and help the organization provide high-quality services to Member Countries.

The programme is particularly relevant to professionals whose careers involve criminal investigations, intelligence analysis, cybercrime, financial crime, border security, organized crime, environmental crime, counter-terrorism, forensics, operational coordination, training, information management and other specialized law enforcement functions.

The vacancy notice identifies the position as the INTERPOL Enhanced Secondment Program, reporting to coordinators within operational directorates. Although the vacancy page identifies Lyon, France as the location of the published opportunity, the detailed vacancy information specifies multiple duty stations, reflecting the international and operational nature of the programme.

Key Details of the Opportunity

  • Opportunity: INTERPOL Enhanced Secondment Programme
  • Organization: INTERPOL
  • Vacancy Notice: 1663
  • Publication starting date: August 2, 2026
  • Location indicated on the vacancy page: Lyon, France
  • Duty stations: Multiple duty stations
  • Duration: 36 months
  • Grade: Grade 5
  • Security clearance: Basic/Enhanced
  • Application deadline: Applications are received throughout the year
  • Eligible applicants: Qualified law enforcement and governmental officials from INTERPOL Member Countries
  • Application route: INTERPOL Recruitment Hub through the organization’s vacancies page
  • Endorsement: Applications must be officially endorsed and submitted through the relevant National Central Bureau (NCB).

What Is the Objective of the INTERPOL Secondment Programme?

The programme aims to establish a pool of vetted law enforcement specialists capable of supporting INTERPOL’s international operational requirements.

The objective is to maintain a dynamic, secure and interoperable global repository of specialists who can provide the right expertise at the right time in response to international crime and policing challenges. This approach enables INTERPOL to strengthen cooperation between Member Countries and improve its ability to coordinate responses to transnational criminal activity.

For participating officers, the programme can also provide exposure to an international working environment where professionals from different national law enforcement systems work together on shared security and criminal justice challenges.

Who Can Apply?

The Enhanced Secondment Programme is specifically targeted at professionals already working within law enforcement and government structures in INTERPOL Member Countries.

Eligible categories identified in the vacancy include:

  1. Active police officers

    Serving police officers can apply where their professional experience and specialization correspond to the operational areas sought by INTERPOL.

  2. Law enforcement officers from national agencies

    This includes professionals working in agencies such as customs, border control and anti-corruption units, as well as other national law enforcement bodies.

  3. Civil servants working in law enforcement or government administrations

    Government officials whose responsibilities are directly connected to law enforcement or relevant national government functions may also be considered.

The vacancy specifically states that the announcement applies to law enforcement and/or governmental officials within INTERPOL Member Countries.

Areas of Expertise Sought

The Enhanced Secondment Programme covers a broad range of criminal justice, policing and operational specialties. Prospective candidates may be considered for different Grade 5 operational positions depending on their professional background and expertise.

Examples include:

Criminal Intelligence Officer

Professionals in this area may contribute to the analysis and dissemination of intelligence concerning transnational crime and support international efforts to identify and respond to criminal threats.

Specialized Officer

Specialized officers may work on particular crime types or specialist operational areas, including fugitives, disaster victim identification, cybercrime, human trafficking and financial crime.

Regional Specialized Officer

These professionals support regional operations by bringing localized knowledge and expertise relevant to particular geographical or operational environments.

Criminal Intelligence Analyst

Criminal intelligence analysts may collect, analyze and interpret criminal-related data and activities while supporting crime prevention and investigative operations.

Crime Areas Covered by the Programme

INTERPOL has identified a broad, non-exhaustive list of crime areas and policing capabilities that candidates can select as areas of interest within their applications.

1. Financial Crimes

Relevant areas include:

  • Anti-corruption
  • Money laundering and asset recovery
  • Fraud and financial crimes
  • Counterfeit currency and security documents

These areas are increasingly important in international law enforcement because financial investigations can reveal criminal networks operating across multiple jurisdictions.

2. Cyber and Digital Forensics

The programme also covers emerging digital crime areas such as:

  • Cybercrime
  • Darknet investigations
  • Cryptocurrency tracing
  • Ransomware analysis
  • Artificial intelligence fraud detection

Professionals with specialized digital investigation and cyber-forensics experience can therefore find their expertise relevant to the programme.

3. Transnational and Organized Crime

This broad category includes:

  • Human trafficking and smuggling networks
  • Online crimes against children
  • War crimes and illicit arms
  • Vehicle crime
  • Drug trafficking
  • Works of art
  • Illicit goods and global health
  • Intellectual property crime and digital piracy
  • Public health and pharmaceutical crime

These areas reflect the international nature of modern organized crime and the need for law enforcement agencies to collaborate across borders.

4. Environmental Crime

Applicants with expertise in environmental enforcement may have experience in:

  • Wildlife crime
  • Fisheries crime
  • Forestry crime
  • Pollution
  • Illegal mining

Environmental crime can involve sophisticated cross-border networks, making international cooperation particularly important.

5. Counter-Terrorism and Extremism

Relevant expertise includes:

  • Counter-terrorism
  • Chemical and explosives terrorism prevention
  • Radiological and nuclear terrorism prevention
  • Bioterrorism prevention

Candidates working in these specialized security areas may therefore find the programme aligned with their professional expertise.

6. Forensics and Bio-Crime

The vacancy identifies several forensic and identification-related areas, including:

  • DNA analysis
  • Biometrics
  • Disaster victim identification
  • Fingerprints and facial recognition
  • Border control
  • Counterfeit currency and security documents

These capabilities can play an important role in international criminal investigations and identification processes.

7. Capacity Building and Training

Professionals with experience in training and institutional development may be considered in areas such as:

  • Training and development
  • Digital curriculum design and operations

This reflects INTERPOL’s emphasis not only on operational investigations but also on strengthening the capabilities of law enforcement institutions.

8. Command and Coordination

The programme also includes expertise in:

  • Operations coordination, planning and support
  • Communication assistance and information management
  • Critical regional operations languages

Professionals in these areas can contribute to coordination between different operational teams and Member Countries.

9. Global Outreach and Regional Assistance

Candidates with experience in international or regional coordination may contribute to:

  • Coordination of regional activities
  • Support to National Central Bureaus

This area is particularly relevant to professionals experienced in working with multiple institutions and stakeholders across jurisdictions.

10. Criminal Intelligence Analysis and Fusion

The programme also seeks expertise in:

  • Collection, analysis and interpretation of criminal-related data and activities
  • Open-source intelligence and analysis

These skills are increasingly important as law enforcement agencies deal with large amounts of structured and unstructured information originating from multiple sources.

Main Duties and Responsibilities

Successful seconded officers will be expected to contribute to INTERPOL’s operational objectives under the supervision and guidance of management.

The responsibilities are designed around addressing specific crime phenomena and supporting coordination of criminal cases and business continuity within existing activities.

Key duties include:

  • Coordinating investigations and cases between Member Countries.
  • Identifying, establishing and maintaining professional contact with experts in relevant fields.
  • Organizing and participating in training programmes.
  • Participating in expert group meetings and conferences.
  • Monitoring and analyzing information relating to the assigned area of activity.
